title: Applying coloured slips to greenware
subtitle: How to brush, dip, and trail coloured liquid clay onto leather-hard stoneware to build surface colour before glazing
excerpt: Coloured slip is liquid clay tinted with metal oxides or commercial stains, applied to unfired clay before the glaze firing. It is the oldest ceramic colouring method and gives results that sit beneath the glaze surface rather than on top of it. The key window for application is the leather-hard stage: too wet and the slip saturates the piece and causes cracking; too dry and the slip does not adhere and flakes off during drying.
sourceNotes: Coloured slip application technique derived from first principles. Slip decoration documented throughout ceramic history; key references include William Burton, A History and Description of English Earthenware and Stoneware (1904) and V&A open-access slipware collection.

content.text: Coloured
slip
is liquid clay stained with colour, applied to
greenware
before the first firing. It is one of the most direct methods of putting colour onto a ceramic surface: the slip fuses into the clay body during
bisque
firing, and a clear or translucent glaze applied on top locks it in and adds depth. The result is colour that reads from beneath the glaze surface, not on it.
The window for application is narrow. Apply slip at the
leather-hard
stage only. Too wet and the slip carries so much moisture that the piece softens and distorts; too dry and the slip sits on the surface without bonding and flakes off during drying.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach. Handle raw oxides with gloves and a respirator. Never near food prep.

content.text: When to use this technique

A good slip coat is even in thickness. It has no pinholes or bare patches. At leather-hard it holds firmly to the surface. Run a fingernail lightly over it. The slip should not lift or flake. After bisque firing the surface is matte and slightly chalky. After a clear glaze firing the colour deepens. The glaze brings out the full richness of the oxide stain.
What you need

Coloured slip is made from the same clay body as the piece it will be applied to (or a closely matching one), mixed with water to a smooth pouring or brushing consistency, and stained with a metal oxide or ceramic stain. For white slip on stoneware: mix 200 g of white stoneware or kaolin into 200 ml of water, stir until smooth, and pass through an 80-mesh sieve. For coloured slip: add ceramic stain powder (typically 5 to 15 percent of dry clay weight) to the base slip and stir well. Common additions include iron oxide for amber and brown tones, cobalt oxide for blue, and copper oxide for green. Wear gloves and a respirator when handling dry oxides. For trailing, you need a slip trailer: a small rubber bulb with a fine nozzle, available from ceramic suppliers, or a plastic squeeze bottle with a fine tip.
Applying coloured slip: step by step

Prepare your greenware: the piece should be at leather-hard. Test by pressing a finger lightly against the clay. The clay should feel cool and slightly damp but should not deform under finger pressure. A piece that is too wet will distort when coated with slip.

Stir the slip thoroughly immediately before use. Slip settles on standing and an unmixed slip will be watery at the top and thick at the bottom, giving an uneven coat. The correct brushing consistency is that of single cream: it runs off a spoon in a slow, even sheet.

For a full-body dip coat: hold the piece at the foot and dip it into the slip to the desired depth in one smooth movement, hold for two seconds, and lift straight out. Place on a banding wheel to check coverage. A dip coat deposits an even, single-thickness layer. One dip coat is usually enough on leather-hard clay.

For brush application: load a hake brush or wide mop brush with slip and apply in broad, even strokes. Work quickly without going back over wet areas: re-stroking wet slip lifts the first coat and creates uneven patches. Two thin coats applied in different directions give more even coverage than one thick coat.
For
slip trailing

: fill the trailer with slip to a thicker consistency than brushing slip, approximately the thickness of double cream. Hold the nozzle 5 mm above the surface and squeeze steadily, moving the trailer at an even pace to lay a raised line. Practise the movement on a tile before working on the piece. Trailing slip dries raised above the clay surface and remains as a texture after firing.

Allow the slip-decorated piece to dry slowly. The added moisture from the slip will cause the clay to soften slightly at the surface: do not handle until the slip coat is firm to the touch, usually 20 to 30 minutes after application. Cover loosely and allow to dry to bone-dry before bisque firing.
What it looks like when it's right

A good slip coat is even in thickness. It has no pinholes or bare patches. At the leather-hard stage it should hold firmly to the surface. Run a fingernail lightly over it: the slip should not lift or flake. After bisque firing, the surface is matte and slightly chalky. After a clear glaze firing, the colour deepens and the glaze brings out the full saturation of the oxide stain.

Trailed slip lines fire to a slightly raised texture that remains tactile under the glaze. On pieces fired to cone 6 with a clear liner glaze, the texture survives intact and can be felt as a fine ridge on the surface.
Common mistakes
Applying slip to bone-dry clay. The slip cannot bond to a surface with no moisture. The result is flaking and peeling as the piece dries. Always apply to leather-hard clay only.

Applying slip that is too thick. Heavy slip deposits crack as the piece dries because the slip shrinks at a different rate from the clay body beneath it. If the slip coat cracks during drying, thin it with water for the next application.

Using a slip body that does not match the clay body. If the slip shrinkage rate differs significantly from the clay body, the slip will crawl off the surface during firing, pulling away in patches. Always match or closely match the clay body in the slip recipe.

Brushing over wet slip too soon. Going back over a wet slip coat with a brush lifts the first layer. Work in one direction, load the brush fully, and apply each stroke once. Let the first coat firm up before applying a second.

Not stirring the slip between uses. Settled slip produces a watery first coat that is too thin, followed by a thick and uneven coat from the concentrated bottom layer. Stir thoroughly every time before loading the brush or trailer.
